title: WHY JESUS CHOSE JUDAS
paragraphs: WHY JESUS CHOSE JUDAS
The room went silent.
The bread was still warm. The wine had not yet been poured. The feet of the disciples were still damp from being washed by the hands of God.
And sitting at that table was a man Jesus already knew would betray Him.
Not suspected.
Not eventually discovered.
Known.
Before Judas ever kissed Jesus in Gethsemane, Jesus already saw the kiss.
Before Judas reached for silver, Jesus already heard the coins.
Before Judas walked into darkness, Jesus already knew the road he would take.
Yet Jesus chose him anyway.
That truth unsettles us.
Because deep down, we want a Savior who only chooses faithful people.
Instead, Scripture reveals a Savior who chooses broken people, weak people, confused people, proud people, doubting people, and even a man who would become history's most infamous betrayer.
Why?
Why would Jesus choose Judas?
The answer reaches far beyond Judas himself.
It reaches into every human heart.
Including yours.
The Mystery Hidden in Plain Sight
When Jesus called His disciples, it was not an accident.
The Gospel of Luke records:
"Καὶ ὅτε ἐγένετο ἡμέρα, προσεφώνησεν τοὺς μαθητὰς αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐκλεξάμενος ἀπ’ αὐτῶν δώδεκα..."
"When day came, He called His disciples and chose from them twelve..." (Luke 6:13)
The Greek word is ἐκλεξάμενος (eklexamenos).
Chosen.
Selected.
Deliberately appointed.
Judas was not a mistake in the selection process.
He was included in the choosing.
Jesus spent the entire night praying before appointing the Twelve.
Entire night.
Every name spoken before the Father.
Every future known.
Every outcome understood.
And still Judas was called.
This means Judas did not slip through divine oversight.
His presence was part of a greater story.
One that reveals both the depth of human sin and the immeasurable glory of God's redemption.
The Scandal Nobody Wants to Admit
Most people read Judas as though he is completely different from them.
They see a villain.
A monster.
A traitor.
But Scripture paints a more uncomfortable picture.
Judas looked like a disciple.
He preached.
He traveled with Jesus.
He witnessed miracles.
He heard every sermon.
He sat at every campfire.
He experienced everything the other disciples experienced.
Nobody suspected him.
At the Last Supper, when Jesus announced that one would betray Him, the disciples did not immediately point at Judas.
Instead they asked:
"Is it I?"
That detail matters.
Judas blended in.
His external life appeared faithful.
His internal life was dying.
That is why Judas remains terrifying.
Not because he was obviously evil.
But because he looked spiritually alive while something hidden was consuming him.
The Gospel writer John gives us a glimpse beneath the surface.
John 12:6 says Judas used to steal from the money bag.
The betrayal in Gethsemane did not begin with silver.
It began years earlier with secret compromise.
Small sins.
Hidden greed.
Private disobedience.
The betrayal was not born in a single night.
It grew in darkness.
This is why Scripture repeatedly warns believers to guard their hearts.
Because what remains unrepented eventually becomes what defines us.
Jesus Knew Everything
One of the most breathtaking moments in Scripture appears in John 6.
After many disciples abandoned Jesus because His teaching was difficult, Jesus turned to the Twelve.
Would they leave too?
Peter answered boldly.
But then Jesus said something astonishing:
"Did I not choose you, the Twelve? Yet one of you is a devil." (John 6:70)
Years before the betrayal.
Years before Gethsemane.
Years before the cross.
Jesus already knew.
The Greek word διάβολος (diabolos) literally means slanderer or accuser.
Jesus was not shocked by Judas.
He was never reacting.
He was always sovereign.
This changes everything.
Because the cross was never God's emergency plan.
It was always His redemptive plan.
The Betrayal That Fulfilled Scripture
Long before Judas was born, Scripture anticipated betrayal.
Psalm 41:9 declares:
"גַּם־אִישׁ שְׁלוֹמִי אֲשֶׁר־בָּטַחְתִּי בוֹ אֹכֵל לַחְמִי הִגְדִּיל עָלַי עָקֵב"
"Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me."
Centuries later Jesus directly applied this passage to Judas.
The betrayal did not prove God lost control.
It proved God had control all along.
Nothing happened outside His sovereign knowledge.
Nothing surprised Heaven.
Nothing altered God's plan of redemption.
The same hands that accepted Judas's betrayal were already preparing salvation for the world.
The Greatest Contrast in the Gospels
Perhaps the most revealing comparison in Scripture is not Judas versus Jesus.
It is Judas versus Peter.
Both failed.
Both sinned.
Both betrayed trust.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Judas betrayed Him for silver.
Yet one became an apostle remembered for faithfulness.
The other became synonymous with betrayal.
Why?
The answer is repentance.
The New Testament uses two important concepts.
Judas experienced remorse.
Peter experienced repentance.
Judas felt horror over what he had done.
Peter ran back to the One he had offended.
Many people confuse guilt with repentance.
They are not the same.
Feeling bad about sin does not save anyone.
Turning to Christ does.
Peter wept.
Judas despaired.
Peter fell into grace.
Judas fell into hopelessness.
One believed his failure was greater than God's mercy.
The other discovered God's mercy was greater than his failure.
That difference changed eternity.
The Question Hidden Inside Judas's Story
The real question is not why Jesus chose Judas.
The real question is why Jesus chooses any of us.
Because every believer has moments of compromise.
Moments of selfishness.
Moments of pride.
Moments of fear.
Moments we wish we could erase.
Scripture says:
"For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God." (Romans 3:23)
All.
Not some.
Not most.
All.
Judas exposes the darkness of the human heart.
But Jesus reveals something even greater.
The power of grace.
The Heart of the Gospel
The Gospel is not the story of good people finding God.
It is the story of God pursuing guilty people.
It is the story of Christ stepping toward sinners when sinners were running from Him.
It is the story of a King who knew exactly what His followers would do and loved them anyway.
Jesus knew Peter would deny Him.
He knew Thomas would doubt Him.
He knew the disciples would flee.
He knew Judas would betray Him.
And still He walked toward the cross.
This is why the Gospel remains the greatest story ever told.
Not because humanity was faithful.
But because Christ was.
The Greek word χάρις (charis) means grace.
Unearned favor.
Undeserved kindness.
Divine generosity given to those who deserve judgment.
Grace is not God pretending sin is insignificant.
Grace is God paying the price Himself.
At Calvary, justice and mercy met.
The innocent died for the guilty.
The Holy One stood where sinners belonged.
The Son of God carried what humanity could never carry.
That is the scandal of grace.
And that is why Jesus rewrites everything.
The Invitation Hidden in Judas's Story
Perhaps the most haunting truth about Judas is that he spent years near Jesus without fully surrendering to Him.
Many people know Christian language.
Christian culture.
Christian routines.
Christian appearances.
Yet Christ does not simply call people to proximity.
He calls them to surrender.
The tragedy of Judas is not merely that he betrayed Jesus.
It is that he remained close enough to hear truth while resisting its transformation.
That warning deserves reflection.
Not condemnation.
Reflection.
Because the question every reader must answer is not whether Judas betrayed Jesus.
The question is whether we have fully entrusted ourselves to the Savior who died and rose again.
The beautiful news of the Gospel is that no one reading these words has to end their story like Judas.
As long as Christ is calling, grace is available.
As long as Christ is calling, forgiveness is available.
As long as Christ is calling, redemption is available.
The empty tomb still announces what the cross accomplished.
No failure is stronger than His mercy.
No sin is greater than His grace.
No past is beyond His power to rewrite.
And perhaps that is why the story of Judas remains in Scripture.
Not so we can merely study a betrayer.
But so we can recognize our need for a Savior.
A Savior who knew exactly what humanity would do to Him.
And chose to love us anyway.
Which part of Judas's story convicted you most?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
The most dangerous place to be is not far from Jesus.
It is close enough to hear Him while refusing to surrender to Him.
